(Entertainment Weekly) -- It was a glass half-full, glass half-empty kind of weekend at the box office for "Funny People," writer-director Judd Apatow's comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death. Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen star in "Funny People," which took the No. 1 slot at the box office this weekend. According to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office, it opened at the top spot with an estimated $23.4 million, better than Apatow's The 40 Year-Old Virgin ($21.4 million) -- hence, the glass is half full. But that figure is far lower than the debut for Apatow's "Knocked Up" ($30.7 million), and it's the worst opening for a comedy for star Adam Sander since his 2000 turkey "Little Nicky" -- hence, the glass is half empty. Of course, "Funny People" was billed more as a thoughtful dramedy than a balls-out Sandler laugh-fest, and when matched against the opening frames for Sandler's serious efforts "Reign Over Me," "Spanglish," and "Punch-Drunk Love," Funny People is far and away the winner -- and the glass is half full again. But whether it's a comedy, drama, or dramedy, "Funny People's" $75 million budget is quite the handful of pretty pennies, and with a shaky "B-" Cinemascore, the film is going to have a hard time overcoming tepid word-of-mouth -- and we're back to the half-empty glass. So let's just move on, shall we? The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, definitely runneth over. Thanks to its debut on IMAX (and the premium ticket prices that come with it), "Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince" came in second with $17.7 million, a soft 40 percent drop from last weekend for $255.5 million total. At this rate, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the 'Potter' franchise. The guinea pigs of "G-Force" were right on its heels at third place, nibbling up $17.1 million, a decent 46 percent drop for a two-week cume of $66.5 million. And Katherine Heigl's romcom "The Ugly Truth" took in an additional $13 million, a 53 percent drop for fourth place and $54.5 million total. Of the two other wide releases this weekend, at least the sci-fi family comedy "Aliens in the Attic" -- which grossed a meager $7.8 million for fifth place -- broke into the top 10. The torture porn flick "The Collector" collected a grisly $3.6 million and plopped dead at 11th place. Box office on a whole was down a massive 22 percent from last year, when The "Dark Knight" and "The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor" both took in over $40 million, but the specialty market showed some vibrant signs of life. Bone fide indie hit "(500) Days of Summer" expanded to 266 theaters for $2.7 million, a $10,338 per theater average. And three widely disparate films opened in four theaters each to healthy per theater averages: The quirky romantic comedy "Adam" ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film "Thirst" ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary "The Cove" ($13,600 per theater). Finally, a true milestone was reached this weekend by "The Hangover." With $5.1 million this weekend for a running total of $255.8 million, the summer's biggest die hard blockbuster has passed "Star Trek" and (for a brief moment) "Harry Potter 6" as the third highest grossing movie of the year. outputs.L1:
**(Entertainment Weekly)** — It was a glass-half-full, glass-half-empty kind of weekend at the box office for *Funny People*, writer-director Judd Apatow’s comedic meditation on fame, humor, life, and death.

Starring Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen, *Funny People* claimed the No. 1 spot with an estimated $23.4 million, according to figures from Hollywood.com Box Office. That opening surpassed Apatow’s *The 40-Year-Old Virgin* ($21.4 million)—hence, the glass is half full.

However, the figure fell well below the $30.7 million debut of Apatow’s *Knocked Up* and marked the worst opening for an Adam Sandler comedy since his 2000 turkey *Little Nicky*—hence, the glass is half empty.

Of course, *Funny People* was marketed more as a thoughtful dramedy than as an all-out Sandler laugh-fest. Compared with the opening weekends of Sandler’s more serious efforts—*Reign Over Me*, *Spanglish*, and *Punch-Drunk Love*—*Funny People* is far and away the winner, making the glass half full once again.

But whether it is considered a comedy, drama, or dramedy, *Funny People* carries a substantial $75 million budget. Coupled with a shaky “B-” CinemaScore, the film may have difficulty overcoming tepid word of mouth—and we are back to the half-empty glass. So let us move on, shall we?

The cup of a certain adolescent wizard, meanwhile, definitely runneth over. Thanks to its IMAX debut—and the premium ticket prices that came with it—*Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince* finished second with $17.7 million. That represented a modest 40 percent decline from the previous weekend and brought its total to $255.5 million. At this rate, the film is well on its way to the upper ranks of the *Potter* franchise.

The guinea pigs of *G-Force* were close behind in third place, nibbling up $17.1 million. That marked a respectable 46 percent drop and brought the film’s two-week cumulative gross to $66.5 million. Katherine Heigl’s romantic comedy *The Ugly Truth* earned an additional $13 million, a 53 percent decline, to finish fourth with a total of $54.5 million.

Of the weekend’s two other wide releases, at least the sci-fi family comedy *Aliens in the Attic*—which grossed a meager $7.8 million for fifth place—managed to break into the top 10. The torture-porn flick *The Collector* collected a grisly $3.6 million and landed dead in 11th place.

The box office as a whole was down a massive 22 percent from the previous year, when *The Dark Knight* and *The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor* each earned more than $40 million. The specialty market, however, showed vibrant signs of life.

Bona fide indie hit *(500) Days of Summer* expanded to 266 theaters and earned $2.7 million, for a per-theater average of $10,338. Three widely disparate films also opened in four theaters apiece, each posting a healthy per-theater average: the quirky romantic comedy *Adam* ($16,566 per theater), the stylish vampire film *Thirst* ($13,793 per theater), and the eco-thriller-cum-documentary *The Cove* ($13,600 per theater).

Finally, *The Hangover* reached a true milestone this weekend. With another $5.1 million, bringing its running total to $255.8 million, the summer’s biggest die-hard blockbuster surpassed *Star Trek* and, briefly, *Harry Potter 6* to become the third-highest-grossing movie of the year.

**CLICK HERE to try two RISK-FREE issues of Entertainment Weekly.**

Copyright 2009 Entertainment Weekly and Time Inc. All rights reserved.

(Entertainment Weekly) — The weekend box-office results for *Funny People*, Judd Apatow’s comic reflection on celebrity, humor, mortality, and life, offered reasons for both optimism and concern.

Starring Adam Sandler and Seth Rogen, the film debuted at No. 1 with an estimated $23.4 million, according to Hollywood.com Box Office. That total surpassed the $21.4 million opening of Apatow’s *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, but fell well short of the $30.7 million earned by *Knocked Up* in its first weekend. It was also Sandler’s weakest comedy debut since the 2000 flop *Little Nicky*.

Still, *Funny People* was promoted as a more contemplative blend of comedy and drama rather than a full-throttle Sandler comedy. Compared with the opening weekends of his more serious films—*Reign Over Me*, *Spanglish*, and *Punch-Drunk Love*—it performed substantially better. On the other hand, the movie cost $75 million to make, and its uncertain “B-” CinemaScore suggested that lukewarm audience reaction could make recouping that investment difficult.

Elsewhere, the outlook was considerably brighter for a certain young wizard. Boosted by its arrival in IMAX theaters and the higher ticket prices associated with the format, *Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince* finished second with $17.7 million. That represented a relatively mild 40 percent decline from the previous weekend and lifted its cumulative earnings to $255.5 million. At that pace, the movie appeared headed toward the top tier of the *Harry Potter* series.

*G-Force* followed closely in third place, collecting $17.1 million. The guinea-pig adventure dropped a respectable 46 percent and reached $66.5 million after two weeks. Katherine Heigl’s romantic comedy *The Ugly Truth* ranked fourth with another $13 million, declining 53 percent and bringing its total to $54.5 million.

Among the weekend’s two other nationwide releases, the family-oriented science-fiction comedy *Aliens in the Attic* at least made the top 10. Its modest $7.8 million placed it fifth. The torture-horror movie *The Collector*, however, managed only $3.6 million and landed in 11th place.

Overall box-office revenue was down a steep 22 percent from the same period a year earlier, when both *The Dark Knight* and *The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor* earned more than $40 million. The specialty-film sector, however, displayed encouraging momentum.

Certified independent success *(500) Days of Summer* expanded into 266 theaters and grossed $2.7 million, averaging $10,338 per location. Three very different movies also opened in four theaters apiece and posted solid per-theater results: the unconventional romance *Adam* averaged $16,566; the visually polished vampire movie *Thirst* averaged $13,793; and the environmental thriller-documentary *The Cove* averaged $13,600.

Finally, *The Hangover* achieved a notable benchmark. Its $5.1 million weekend raised its total to $255.8 million, allowing the summer’s biggest durable blockbuster to overtake *Star Trek* and, briefly, *Harry Potter 6* as the year’s third-highest-grossing film.

The weekend box office was judged not only by each film’s rank, but also by its opening gross, week-to-week decline, production budget, audience reaction, and the track records of the filmmakers and stars involved.

Universal’s “Funny People” opened at No. 1 with an estimated $23.4 million. Although that was enough to win the weekend, the result was modest for an Adam Sandler comedy and troubling for a film that reportedly cost about $75 million to produce. Writer-director Judd Apatow’s earlier movies had benefited from strong reviews and sustained word of mouth, but “Funny People” received a “B-” CinemaScore from opening-night audiences. Combined with the film’s long running time and darker tone, that response suggested it might not have the staying power needed to become profitable domestically. Its debut also fell below those of several recent Sandler releases and Apatow’s “Knocked Up,” though it was slightly ahead of the opening for “The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” a far less expensive production.

“Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince” remained solid in second place, bringing its domestic total to $255.5 million. While the fantasy sequel had declined sharply after its enormous opening, it continued to attract a broad audience and was already one of the summer’s biggest hits. Its strong overseas business further reinforced the franchise’s value.

Elsewhere, holdover films continued to compete for family and adult audiences. “G-Force” performed well among families, while the romantic comedy “The Ugly Truth” showed respectable staying power. The new family release “Aliens in the Attic,” however, opened softly and faced an uphill battle. Overall, the weekend demonstrated that a first-place finish alone does not guarantee success: costs, audience enthusiasm, competition, and long-term momentum can matter as much as the opening number itself.

## Domestic box-office recap: July 31–August 2, 2009

Judd Apatow’s **“Funny People”** led the domestic box office, but its approximately **$22.7 million** debut was modest considering its cast, marketing and reported **$75 million production budget**. The R-rated, 146-minute comedy-drama opened in **3,008 theaters**, averaging about **$7,500 per location**.

The result was enough for first place, though Universal had initially projected a weekend closer to $23 million. Its more serious tone, long running time and mixed audience response likely kept it from matching the broader appeal of Apatow’s earlier comedies.

### Top domestic films

| Rank | Film | Weekend gross | Change | Domestic total |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | **Funny People** | **$22.7M** | New | $22.7M |
| 2 | **Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince** | **$17.9M** | -39% | $255.5M |
| 3 | **G-Force** | **$17.5M** | -45% | $66.9M |
| 4 | **The Ugly Truth** | **$13.0M–$13.2M** | about -52% | roughly $54.5M |
| 5 | **Aliens in the Attic** | **$8.0M** | New | $8.0M |
| 6 | **Orphan** | **$7.5M** | about -41% | roughly $26.7M |
| 7 | **Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs** | **$5.5M** | about -34% | roughly $181.8M |
| 8 | **The Hangover** | **$5.2M** | about -20% | roughly $255.8M |
| 9 | **The Proposal** | **$4.9M** | about -24% | roughly $149M |
| 10 | **Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen** | **$4.6M** | about -42% | roughly $388M |

The holdovers generally performed as expected. **“Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince”** recovered from its steep second-weekend fall and declined a more manageable 39% in its third frame. It narrowly stayed ahead of Disney’s **“G-Force,”** which fell about 45%.

The Katherine Heigl–Gerard Butler romantic comedy **“The Ugly Truth”** suffered a sharper second-weekend decline of roughly 52%, though its $54 million-plus running total remained solid. Warner Bros.’ horror release **“Orphan”** held somewhat better, falling about 41%.

The weekend’s other major newcomer, Fox’s family comedy **“Aliens in the Attic,”** opened to only **$8 million**, a weak start for a nationwide effects-driven release.

Two summer comedies continued to show strong legs. **“The Hangover”** slipped only about 20% in its ninth weekend and moved beyond $255 million domestically, while **“The Proposal”** declined roughly 24% and approached $150 million.

## How “Funny People” compared with Apatow’s films

As a director, Apatow had previously opened:

- **“The 40-Year-Old Virgin”** — about **$21.4 million** in 2005  
- **“Knocked Up”** — about **$30.7 million** in 2007  
- **“Funny People”** — about **$22.7 million** in 2009  

Thus, “Funny People” opened slightly above “The 40-Year-Old Virgin,” but well below “Knocked Up.” The comparison was not especially encouraging because “Virgin” had been a less expensive breakout movie that benefited from exceptional word of mouth, eventually reaching about **$109 million domestically**. “Knocked Up” finished near **$149 million**.

“Funny People,” by contrast, was marketed as a star-driven summer event and carried a much higher budget. Its combination of stand-up comedy, mortality and troubled relationships made it less accessible than Apatow’s earlier films, leaving it dependent on unusually strong legs to become a comparable domestic success.

## How it compared with Adam Sandler’s openings

For Adam Sandler, the debut was far below the openings of most of his mainstream comedies from the preceding decade. Recent examples included:

- **“You Don’t Mess with the Zohan”** — about **$38.5 million**
- **“I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry”** — about **$34.2 million**
- **“Click”** — about **$40 million**
- **“The Longest Yard”** — about **$47.6 million**
- **“50 First Dates”** — about **$39.9 million**
- **“Anger Management”** — about **$42.2 million**
- **“Bedtime Stories”** — about **$27.5 million**

“Funny People” was closer to Sandler’s dramatic or off-brand projects than to his broad studio comedies. It did outperform the wide-opening results of films such as **“Reign Over Me”** and **“Spanglish,”** but its $22.7 million launch ranked among the softer starts of his modern star period.

The opening also underscored the difficulty of selling Sandler in a darker, more self-reflective role. Audiences expecting one of his conventional high-concept comedies instead found a long, R-rated story about a successful comedian confronting illness and personal failure.

## Specialty and independent releases

The strongest indie story remained Fox Searchlight’s **“(500) Days of Summer.”** Expanding to roughly **266 theaters**, the romantic comedy earned about **$3.7 million**, an excellent per-theater average of approximately **$14,000**. It placed just outside the top ten and demonstrated strong crossover potential as it continued its platform rollout.

Kathryn Bigelow’s **“The Hurt Locker”** also expanded, reaching more than **500 theaters** and taking in roughly **$1.9 million**. Its domestic total moved toward **$10 million**—still modest in absolute terms, but impressive for an independently distributed Iraq War drama.

Among smaller specialty titles:

- The documentary **“The Cove”** expanded to several dozen theaters and earned roughly a quarter-million dollars.
- Armando Iannucci’s political satire **“In the Loop”** continued its limited rollout with healthy art-house averages.
- Park Chan-wook’s vampire film **“Thirst”** opened in four theaters with approximately **$50,000**, averaging more than **$12,000 per site**.

Overall, “Funny People” won the weekend but did not produce the kind of commanding debut normally associated with an Adam Sandler summer comedy. The opening was respectable for an adult, R-rated dramedy, yet underwhelming relative to its cost, pedigree and the commercial records of both Sandler and Apatow.
